basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan's overall food self-sufficiency rate (calorie basis) was 30.3% in 2023 (18-year low) and 30.7% in 2024 (Ministry of Agriculture / Agriculture and Food Agency 糧食供需年報, via Focus Taiwan, Taipei Times, 上下游新聞); grain self-sufficiency 25.5% in 2023 vs 26.6% in 2022; rice self-sufficiency near 100% (97.7% in 2023, 24万公頃/~1.21M tonnes/yr); wheat ~0.3%, soybean <1%, feed corn ~2.5% self-sufficient, ~8M tonnes coarse grain imported yearly (SETN, 農傳媒); legal rice reserve minimum 3 months/25% of consumption since 2006, above FAO's 17-18% and Japan/Korea targets, actual stock ~1.06M tonnes (~11 months) per Dec 2025 CNA report; WTO rice import TRQ of 144,720 tonnes/year since 2002 accession; 大糧倉計畫 (Grand Grain Silo plan) since 2016 paying farmers to convert paddies to soybean/feed corn, expanded 2022; Typhoon Krathon Oct 2024 vegetable wholesale price NT$63.7/kg then -17% to NT$52.8/kg (Taiwan News); 2023 rice harvest hurt by irrigation suspension, Typhoon Koinu, winter monsoon. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: A typhoon hits Taiwan. Supermarket shelves look empty for a few days, and prices jump fast. Have you ever wondered what happens the next time?
slides.2: SDG 2 is not only about hunger far away. It means food security: enough safe food, every day, for all of us. That includes Taiwan too.
slides.3: Taiwan has about 23 million people. Most of our food actually arrives here by ship. In 2024, we grew only 30.7 percent of our own food.
slides.4: That number keeps declining. It dropped to 30.3 percent in 2023, the lowest level in 18 years. It only rose a little after that year.
slides.5: Look closer, and the picture splits. Rice is almost 100 percent homegrown here. But total grain self-sufficiency is only 25.5 percent. That's because most wheat comes from abroad.
slides.6: So your rice grew here in Taiwan. Your bread almost never did. Even the pig that became your lunch probably ate imported corn instead.
slides.7: Here is some good news for once. Rice covers about 240,000 hectares of Taiwan. Two harvests a year produce roughly 1.21 million tonnes of rice.
slides.8: The law protects our rice too. Taiwan must always keep a rice reserve for three whole months. That target is higher than Japan's own goal.
slides.9: Back in 2016, a new government plan actually started. People simply call it the Grand Grain Silo. It pays farmers well to grow soybean instead.
slides.10: Some rice fields used to sit unused after harvest. Today, growers can actually choose to plant corn there instead. That empty ground finally has a purpose again.
slides.11: Researchers here are also testing something quite new. They feed pigs with local feed rice instead of imported corn. It's a small step, but a real one.
slides.12: But this is not a free win for anyone. Soybean grown here is far more expensive than soybean bought abroad. Someone always has to pay that extra cost.
slides.13: Farmers everywhere sell grain to the cheapest buyer. That is normal, and it works well most years. That is why almost nobody notices our heavy import numbers.
slides.14: But global trade rules do not actually bend for us. Since 2002, Taiwan must import rice every year. That happens even when our own stock is already full.
slides.15: The buffer is thinner than it looks. Before Typhoon Krathon struck in 2024, vegetable prices jumped fast. They fell back only once the storm had passed.
slides.16: So cheap imports keep our prices low most years. But they leave very little room for the year when trouble suddenly strikes twice, both here and abroad.
slides.17: To sum up, Taiwan holds two numbers at once. Rice sits near 100 percent, almost every single year. Everything else sits near only 30 percent instead.
slides.18: This choice is not someone else's problem. Future engineers and farm planners will decide this. Maybe some of you will decide how much extra safety Taiwan buys.
slides.19: So try this one simple habit. Think about where your dinner actually came from. Notice it whenever a new farm rule shows up online.
slides.20: A full plate today does not promise a full plate tomorrow. It never does. Let's not wait for an empty shelf before we finally ask why.
